extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and policy observers interested in censorship and media regulation
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of censorship: definitions, historical examples, mechanisms (state and private), measurement indices, types and tactics, and the interplay with surveillance and self-regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom House / Freedom of the Press
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship for individual countries is measured by Freedom House (Freedom of the Press) as one of the comparative metrics for national press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a country-level comparative index alongside other measures to assess press freedom and censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters Without Borders / Press Freedom Index
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters Without Borders publishes a Press Freedom Index used to measure national levels of media censorship and press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the principal comparative measures referenced for assessing censorship by country (used together with Freedom House, V-Dem, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: V-Dem government censorship effort index
rubrics_metrics.description: V-Dem provides a government censorship effort index to quantify state-level censorship activity and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an empirical metric of governmental censorship intensity in comparative research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom on the Net
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom on the Net is a metric used to measure aspects of internet freedom and censorship in individual countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often cited for country-level assessments of internet censorship and restrictions on online expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: OpenNet Initiative (ONI) classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: OpenNet Initiative classifications are used to categorize technical filtering and internet censorship practices in countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ONI focuses on technical filtering; because of legal/ethical concerns it does not check for filtering of child pornography and therefore its classifications focus on technical filtering rather than all types of suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry self-regulation (parental/age ratings and warnings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industries have used self-regulatory warning and rating systems (e.g., Parental Advisory for music, ESRB for video games, MPAA for films, TV Parental Guidelines) as concessions to deter government censorship or legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These systems are described as concessions made by industries to avoid legislative oversight; they function as preventive mechanisms and are considered in analyses of how societies manage content without direct state bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: State censorship apparatus presence and integration (Glavlit example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence and embedding of state censorship bodies within media institutions (e.g., the Soviet Glavlit with censors present in publishing houses and editorial staffs) is a criterion for evaluating the scope and thoroughness of state censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include central censorship agencies, numbers of censors, and direct placement of censors in media organizations, showing comprehensive control over mass media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privishing (deliberate under-publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Privishing: when a publisher under pressure technically publishes a work but deliberately orders a very small print run and makes minimal publicity efforts, effectively suppressing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a subtle form of suppression used to avoid legal or political consequences while denying a work wide circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle suppression via labeling works 'subversive' or 'inconvenient'
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities may justify suppressing knowledge of a document or restricting its dissemination by declaring it 'subversive' or 'inconvenient'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an indirect tactic of censorship; examples and scholarly discussion (e.g., Foucault's case) illustrate how labeling enables suppression without transparent legal process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling effect / surveillance-induced self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where surveillance does not directly censor content, the widespread belief or knowledge of being surveilled can create a 'chilling effect' that leads to self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes surveillance from censorship and highlights an important indirect mechanism by which expression is curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated social media censorship predictors (findings by Gary King et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical patterns of automated social media censorship: posts mentioning the government are not deleted more or less often based on being supportive or critical; posts mentioning collective action are more likely to be deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate what content automated censorship systems target; indicates state priorities (e.g., preventing organization/collective action) rather than simple suppression of criticism per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform localization and shadowbanning (TikTok example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform code and localized guidelines can categorize hashtags and restrict interaction (shadowbanning); localized content moderation can increase censorship of certain social movements or identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shadowbanned hashtags referencing movements or LGBTQ identity; analysts warn localization of guidelines may increase censorship across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content manipulation for political/cultural purpose (weather reports, art bans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-obvious domains (e.g., weather forecasts, artworks, exhibitions) can be manipulated or banned to avoid political embarrassment or to shape public memory (e.g., doctored weather reports in Eastern Bloc; bans on politically significant art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that censorship and content manipulation extend beyond overtly political texts to everyday factual reporting and cultural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship tactic: redaction and censor bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Redaction and censor bars are basic, visible forms of removing sensitive information from documents to allow distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a basic form of censorship often used to permit distribution of otherwise sensitive material by removing identifying or sensitive segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deplatforming and denial-of-access tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Deplatforming: denying access to a platform to express opinions, used as a means to silence or reduce visibility of speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among types of censorship and suppression tactics (affects individual ability to reach audiences even if not legally banned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation intended to silence critics (SLAPP) is categorized as a tactic used to censor or intimidate by imposing legal and financial burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered a non-technical but effective censorship method used to deter criticism through legal pressure rather than direct content removal.
